query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles produced under rapid heating and cooling, the selection of a single-phase solid-solution state is governed by a transient high-temperature diffusion state. A brief thermal hold just below the melting point enhances atomic mobility, enabling sufficient mixing to overcome kinetic barriers, and thereby prevents phase separation and elemental segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Noble metal-based HEA nanoparticle precursors containing more than five elements, initially processed via rapid heating and cooling regimes that typically yield mixed phases with segregation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, brief thermal hold at a temperature just below the full melting point during the synthesis process to extend the high-temperature state before rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied within processing regimes characterized by rapid heating and cooling (e.g., laser ablation synthesis) at temperatures near decomposition; the hold time must be short enough to avoid excessive coarsening yet sufficient to promote atomic diffusion.
generation.structural_mediator: A transient liquid-like state or a high-diffusivity regime that mediates atomic rearrangement across the constituent elements.
generation.mechanism: The short thermal hold increases atomic mobility by extending the high-temperature state, thereby enabling a more uniform distribution of elements. This mitigates kinetic trapping associated with rapid quenching, reducing elemental segregation and phase separation while favoring the formation of a homogenous single-phase solid solution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles synthesized with the thermal hold will display a more uniform single-phase solid-solution crystal structure, with reduced signs of phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled particle morphology compared to samples processed with immediate quenching.
generation.baseline: Standard synthesis using rapid heating followed by immediate rapid cooling, which typically results in phase separation, elemental segregation, and non-uniform particle morphology.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to noble metal-based HEA nanoparticles with more than five constituent elements synthesized under rapid thermal processing conditions. It holds when the processing temperature is near the decomposition point and the thermal hold duration is optimized to facilitate mixing without causing significant particle coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal temperature and hold duration for maximized atomic mixing remain to be determined, and the influence of subtle variations in elemental diffusivities on phase stability requires further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of noble metal-based HEA nanoparticles under identical rapid heating and cooling conditions, differing only in that one set incorporates a controlled thermal hold at a temperature just below the full melting point. Characterize both sets using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase analysis and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for elemental distribution.
measurements: XRD to assess phase purity and solid-solution formation
TEM imaging to determine particle morphology and size distribution
EDS mapping to evaluate elemental homogeneity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles synthesized with the thermal hold do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in single-phase solid-solution formation and elemental homogeneity, compared to the baseline immediate-quench samples, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

Design and Development of High-Entropy Alloys with a Tailored Composition and Phase Structure Based on Thermodynamic Parameters and Film Thickness Using a Novel Combinatorial Target

Abstract: This study presents a novel synthesis route for high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and high-entropy metallic glass (HEMG) using radio frequency (RF) magnetron sputtering and controlling the HEA phase selection according to atomic size difference (δ) and film thickness. The preparation of HEAs using sputtering requires either multitargets or the preparation of a target containing at least five distinct elements. In developing HEA-preparation techniques, the emergence of a novel sputtering target system is promising to prepare a wide range of HEAs. A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

The Effect of Electronic Structure on the Phases Present in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractMulticomponent systems, termed High Entropy Alloys (HEAs), with predominantly single solid solution phases are a current area of focus in alloy development. Although different empirical rules have been introduced to understand phase formation and determine what the dominant phases may be in these systems, experimental investigation has revealed that in many cases their structure is not a single solid solution phase, and that the rules may not accurately distinguish the stability of the phase boundaries. Here, a combined modelling and experimental approach that looks into the electronic structure is proposed to improve accuracy of the predictions of the majority phase. To do this, the Rigid Band model is generalised for magnetic systems in prediction of the majority phase most likely to be found. Good agreement is found when the predictions are confronted with data from experiments, including a new magnetic HEA system (CoFeNiV).
